raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy for patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF), typically with reduced or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), narrow QRS duration, and persistent symptoms despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). Contemporary HF guidelines emphasize foundational pharmacotherapy and established device therapies, particularly implantable defibrillators and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) in appropriately selected patients [1,2]. However, many symptomatic patients have QRS durations below CRT thresholds, and trials of CRT in narrow-QRS HF have been neutral or harmful, defining a therapeutic gap that motivated CCM development [3,4].

CCM delivers relatively high-voltage, non-excitatory biphasic impulses to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period; the signal does not trigger a new depolarization but modifies myocardial contractile biology [5]. Early translational work showed acute improvement in left ventricular performance in canine HF models, followed by longer-term attenuation of progressive remodeling [6,7]. In humans with advanced HF and normal QRS duration, acute and short-term studies showed feasibility and signals of improved exercise capacity and quality of life [8]. Mechanistically, CCM appears to enhance contractility without the energetic penalty typical of catecholaminergic inotropy: paired animal–human studies found increased LV function without increased myocardial oxygen consumption [10]. Chronic therapy has been associated with reverse molecular remodeling, including normalization of fetal-gene expression and upregulation of calcium-handling genes such as SERCA2a, phospholamban, and ryanodine receptor pathways [9,11]. Imaging studies further suggest improvements in global and regional systolic function and LV reverse remodeling rather than resynchronization per se [12].

Clinical evidence has evolved through the FIX-HF program. The randomized double-blind FIX-HF-4 crossover trial enrolled symptomatic patients with LVEF ≤35% and showed improvements in quality-of-life measures, although co-primary endpoints were not uniformly met [13]. FIX-HF-5 was designed as a larger randomized trial in advanced HF and established procedural feasibility and safety; the overall trial missed its primary efficacy endpoint, but prespecified and subsequent analyses identified greater benefit in patients with NYHA class III symptoms and LVEF ≥25% [14-16]. This observation led to FIX-HF-5C, which randomized patients with NYHA III/ambulatory IV symptoms, QRS <130 ms, and LVEF 25–45% to CCM plus GDMT versus GDMT alone. At 24 weeks, CCM improved peak VO₂, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire score, NYHA class, and 6-minute walk distance, with acceptable device-related safety [17]. A subsequent two-lead Optimizer Smart system study demonstrated similar safety and performance while simplifying implantation by eliminating the atrial lead requirement [18].

Beyond randomized trials, pragmatic questions include dosing, durability, and real-world outcomes. A randomized comparison of 5 versus 12 hours/day suggested that shorter daily delivery may be sufficient, though data were preliminary [19]. Longer observational studies reported sustained improvements in functional class, exercise capacity, and quality of life over 2 years [20], and multicenter long-term experience with the Optimizer Smart system suggested durable symptomatic benefit and acceptable safety [21]. Meta-analyses have generally concluded that CCM improves functional capacity and patient-reported outcomes, while effects on mortality and HF hospitalization remain less certain because existing trials were modest in size and follow-up duration [22,23].

Patient selection is therefore central. The best-supported profile is chronic symptomatic HF despite optimized GDMT, sinus rhythm or adequate rhythm-sensing conditions, LVEF approximately 25–45%, QRS <130 ms, and no conventional CRT indication. Patients with very advanced HF, severe right-sided disease, high ventricular ectopy limiting signal delivery, mechanical tricuspid valves, or need for frequent device interactions require individualized assessment. CCM may be particularly relevant in HF with mildly reduced EF at the lower range and in CRT-ineligible HFrEF, but evidence remains strongest for symptomatic NYHA class III patients [24,25].

Implementation resembles transvenous pacemaker implantation but requires expertise in septal lead placement, device programming, interaction testing with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and follow-up troubleshooting [26]. Recent reviews emphasize that CCM should be viewed as complementary—not competitive—to GDMT, defibrillator therapy, CRT when indicated, cardiac rehabilitation, and advanced HF therapies [27,28]. Mechanistic work continues to explore calcium handling, beta-adrenergic signaling, metabolic remodeling, fibrosis, and inflammatory pathways as determinants of response [29,30]. The major unmet need is adequately powered, sham-controlled trials with contemporary GDMT that evaluate hard outcomes, durability, cost-effectiveness, and responder phenotypes. Until then, CCM is best considered for carefully selected symptomatic patients in whom conventional evidence-based therapies have been optimized but functional limitation persists.
